questions.prompt: Which of these statements defines effective radiative forcing (ERF)?
author: Erin Raif
options: The magnitude of net downward radiative flux at the top of atmosphere at a given time
The change in net downward radiative flux at the top of atmosphere over the industrial period
The change in net downward radiative flux at the top of atmosphere caused by a radiative perturbation to the Earth system excluding any other changes to the Earth system
The change in net downward radiative flux at the top of atmosphere caused by a radiative perturbation to the Earth including adjustments to the atmosphere without a change in surface temperature

questions.prompt: Two aerosol species produce identical global mean effective radiative forcing. Which statement is most accurate?
questions.answer: The same global mean forcing can produce different regional climate responses because aerosol location, absorption characteristics, and atmospheric adjustments influence circulation and precipitation patterns.
author: Ken Carslaw
options: Their temperature responses must be identical everywhere
Their regional precipitation responses may differ substantially
Their forcing efficacies must be identical
Their cloud responses must be identical

questions.prompt: Which of the following equations defines the equilibrium climate sensitivity? \(\lambda\) is the climate sensitivity parameter in \(\mathrm{K/Wm^{-2}}\), \(\Delta F\) is a radiative forcing, and \(\Delta T\) is the change in global mean surface temperature.
questions.answer: ECS is defined as the change in global mean surface temperature at equilibrium after a doubling of atmospheric CO\(_2\) concentration. The radiative forcing associated with a doubling of CO\(_2\) is \(\Delta F_{2\times CO_2}\), and the climate sensitivity parameter \(\lambda\) relates the forcing to the temperature response. ECS is a misonomer in that it is actually a temperature (in K) rather than a sensitivity.
author: Ken Carslaw

questions.prompt: Which of the following equations defines the efficacy of a radiative forcing agent \(f\)?
questions.answer: The efficacy of a radiative forcing is defined as the change in global mean surface temperature per unit radiative forcing relative to a doubling of CO\(_2\).
author: Ken Carslaw
options: \({\rm Efficacy}_f = (\Delta T_f/\Delta F_f)/(\Delta T_{2 \times CO_2}/\Delta F_{2\times CO_2})\)

questions.prompt: The effective radiative forcing of CO\(_2\) is approximately 2 W m\(^2\) over the industrial period. This is about 5% of the effect of all CO\(_2\) in the atmosphere (35 W m\(^{-2}\) if all naturally occurring CO\(_2\) were removed). What is the equivalent approximate percentage for the effect of anthropogenic aerosols in the cloud-free part of the atmosphere?
questions.answer: The anthropogenic aerosol radiative forcing under cloud-free conditions is very uncertain, but is of the order -0.4 W m\(^{-2}\). In the natural atmosphere, aerosols reflect about 4 W m\(^{-2}\) (Fig. 2.6), so the answer is about 10%.
author: Ken Carslaw

questions.prompt: Long-term measurements of surface solar radiation provide one line of evidence for the effect of anthropogenic aerosols on Earth's energy budget. Over a polluted region like Europe, by approximately how much did surface solar radiation decline from the 1950s to the 1980s?
questions.answer: Compilation of long-term measurements over Europe show a decline of a few percent in surface solar radiation. See Fig 2.3.
author: Ken Carslaw
options: A possible decline, but difficult to detect above natural variability
A decline of a fraction of a percent
A decline of a few percent

questions.prompt: An Arctic stratus cloud has a cloud droplet number concentration \(N_\mathrm{d}\) of 20 cm\(^{-3}\). A subtropical cumulus cloud \(N_\mathrm{d}\) = 120 cm\(^{-3}\). A parcel of dry air containing 20 cm\(^{-3}\) of aerosol is entrained into the cloud. Assuming all these aerosols act as CCN and nucleate, the total liquid water content of the cloud is approximately constant, and that within a cloud, the droplets are of the same size, calculate:
questions.answer: Reflectivity scales with \(\sqrt[3]{N_\mathrm{d}}\). To calculate the fractional change, we can do \(\sqrt[3]{\frac{N_\mathrm{old}+N_\mathrm{new}}{N_\mathrm{old}}}\), where \(N_\mathrm{old}\) is the droplet number before the entrainment and \(N_\mathrm{new}\) is the droplet number after the entrainment.
